lines: -I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

+I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait for the late shuttle, so my reading of the pilot data is personal as well as analytical. The record shows 160 boardings in week A and 240 in week B [@lyra:1]. Those figures count trips, not unique students, and no attendance data were collected [@lyra:1]. The increase therefore reflects service usage during those specific weeks, not a causal shift in class participation or a broader change in student behavior.

-My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

+Two design choices limit what the boarding counts can support. First, the two weeks differed in academic schedule, so the observed rise in trips may track class days rather than shuttle use. Second, the pilot was not randomized; students were not assigned to ride or not ride, so any difference in boardings cannot be attributed to the shuttle itself. Without controlled conditions or attendance data, the increase remains correlational. I cannot claim the shuttle caused higher participation. I can only say someone rode more often in week B, and that fact does not answer whether more students came to class.

+The survey faces the same representational problem. The 18 responses came solely from voluntary shuttle riders [@lyra:2]. Because non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2], these answers describe existing users, not the wider student population. This qualitative gap leaves unmeasured demand unaddressed. Taken with the quantitative limitations, these combined omissions justify a conditional extension to gather better data, rather than supporting a final policy decision based on the current evidence.

+I recommend extending the pilot for one term to close the sampling gap. The current data cannot confirm whether the service affects attendance, so the extension should function as a study period rather than a validation of success. Since non-riders were excluded from the initial survey [@lyra:2], the next phase must prioritize measuring their access and preferences. We should avoid drawing causal conclusions or claiming financial impacts, as no cost data exists [@lyra:2]. This one-term window allows the committee to test whether the shuttle actually serves the broader student body.

+To fulfill this priority, we should collect brief feedback from students who did not ride, asking specifically about barriers such as schedule mismatches, stop locations, or awareness issues. We must avoid inventing cost or emissions figures, since no such measurements were taken in the original pilot [@lyra:2]. Instead, the focus should remain on practical access questions: who tried to use the service but could not, and why? This approach keeps the evidence grounded in what we can actually observe rather than speculating about expenses or environmental impacts. The resulting data will show whether the current route structure meets real student needs or merely serves those already inclined to ride.
